summary: Lewis County, WA D-6 cupola lookout on The Rockies, built 1929; 1941 bomber crash, 1942-43 aircraft warning use, removed or destroyed 1956.

facts.status_note: Removed or destroyed in 1956 (sources differ on the word). Sources describe an overgrown trail and debris near the summit, not standing structures.

visit.trail_note: Guide: approach by FR 74 (gravel, rough in places; the easiest route described needs 4WD high clearance), then an overgrown route with an easy-to-follow final stretch to the former lookout. Ownership is mixed; check with land managers.

events.note: Wallace Mead named as lookout at the site, with a phone line (Chehalis Bee-Nugget, July 1922)
Rainier National Forest recommended $1,000 for a lookout house; whether it built the 1929 cabin is not stated
D-6 cupola cabin built, per the Lookout Inventory cited by the guide and the register
Forest Service employee Senter died after a shooting accident near Morton; sources disagree on first name (Herman or Thurman) and on whether he was the lookout
Twin-motored bomber (McChord Field or Army Air Corps) crashed near the summit, wreckage over about two acres
Site used by the Aircraft Warning Service, active April 6, 1942 to October 16, 1943
Register says the cabin was eventually removed
firelookout.com and the guide say the cabin was destroyed
Registered October 17, 2010, nominated by Irene Potter

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register says the cabin was eventually removed in 1956. firelookout.com and the guide say it was destroyed that year. The story reports both words and does not say how the cabin ended.

The Oregonian item, as quoted on the Forest Lookouts page, calls the man Herman Senter, a forest ranger. The Centralia Daily Chronicle report calls him Thurman Senter, 29, a Forest Service employee. The guide calls him the lookout in 1931, but the Centralia report places him building cabins about four miles from the lookout station. The sources do not settle the name or his role.

A 1923 newspaper item says the Rainier National Forest recommended $1,000 for a lookout house, but the register and guide give 1929 for the D-6 cabin. The sources do not say whether an earlier structure stood on the site.
The register and firelookout.com place the site in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest. The Forest Lookouts page lists the Snoqualmie National Forest.

notes_for_editor: Brief access was 'unknown' and no access level is set: the sources describe routes and ownership but no closure or permission rule. Check with the Gifford Pinchot National Forest before setting an access level. The Forest Lookouts page quotes a 1931 Oregonian item with the first name Herman and a Centralia Daily Chronicle report with Thurman; the story keeps both. The 1941 bomber is called a McChord Field plane in one source and an Army Air Corps bomber in another. No photos were added because no license information was found for the photo captions on these pages.
